This same many-to-one collision class (a shared-key population with a one-direction-only uniqueness guard) should be checked for in any OTHER crosswalk or fuzzy-match logic in this codebase -- this card fixed Williamson's situs crosswalk specifically; it did not audit for the same pattern elsewhere.

LESSON: A uniqueness guard computed via count(*) OVER (PARTITION BY X) only proves uniqueness from X's own side. A join with two independently-populated sides needs the guard checked from BOTH sides' partition keys, or it silently admits many-to-one collisions that look individually clean from the side that was checked.

When a fix's uniqueness guard must be correct across a CHUNKED/PAGED execution, the guard's own denominator (here, situs-sharing multiplicity) must be computed against the FULL population, never just the current page's batch -- a colliding sibling can land in a different chunk and be invisible to a batch-scoped guard.

A corrective reset scoped to 'provably crosswalk-sourced cells' (own-row field is null) is strictly more defensible than a blanket reset of 'every exposed account's cells' -- it excludes native CAD data automatically and correctly, as demonstrated by marketValue surviving the reset on the traced pair.

After a reset-then-rerun sequence, the re-run's OTHER (unrelated) logic can produce a more precise result than what was reset to -- here, R6 cad-null-verified turned a reset 'unaccounted' into a more informative 'absent-verified' on the very next run. Don't treat a dispatch's predicted end-state as gospel if the actual result is honestly better; report the discrepancy and why.

Sizing a 'sweep' as both 'merely exposed' and 'actually collided' before remediating is valuable even when (as here) the two numbers turn out identical (134=134) -- the sizing work is what let the marketValue-vs-crosswalk-fields distinction be caught cleanly afterward, since the byRail breakdown was already in hand for comparison.
